title: Reflexive Pronouns
subtitle: When the person doing it and the person it happens to are the same.
objectives: Explain how a reflexive pronoun differs from an intensive one
Use reflexive pronouns correctly as objects
Recognise verbs that do not take a reflexive pronoun in English
Retell the windmills episode and explain what Don Quixote concludes

cards.title: Same eight words. Completely different job
cards.text: Last week they added emphasis. This week they are doing real work, and taking them out breaks the sentence.

cards.title: The subject and the object are the same person
cards.text: A reflexive pronoun is used when whoever does the action is also on the receiving end of it.
points: **"He hurt *himself*."** He is both doer and receiver.
**"She taught *herself*."** Same person, both ends.
**Without it the verb has no object.**
**Taught who? Hurt who?** The sentence needs an answer.

cards.title: Cross it out and see what survives
cards.text: Compare the first two tabs. One sentence survives the deletion and one does not.

question.text: Which sentence uses a REFLEXIVE pronoun?
options: She cut herself on the tin
question.explain: Cut who? Herself is the object. In the other three the word could be removed.

cards.title: One question tells you which it is
cards.text: Take the -self word out. If the sentence still makes sense, it was intensive. If it breaks, it was reflexive.
points: **"He hurt."** Broken. So it was reflexive.
**"The captain apologised."** Fine. So it was intensive.
**Ten seconds**, and it works every time.
**Same eight words.** Only the job changes.

cards.title: Most of what you learn, you teach yourself
cards.text: A coach shows you once. The thousand repetitions afterwards are you doing it to yourself, which is exactly the grammar.
points: **"He trained *himself*"** — doer and receiver.
**"He trained"** on its own means something looser.
**The reflexive makes it deliberate.**
**A small word, and it changes the claim.**

question.explain: Itself. Washed who? The cat. Doer and receiver are the same, so it is reflexive.

cards.title: Some verbs do not take one, and it sounds wrong if you add it
cards.text: Many languages use a reflexive where English does not. These are the ones that catch people out.
points: **"I feel tired."** Not *I feel myself tired*.
**"He got up."** Not *he got himself up*.
**"She concentrated."** Not *concentrated herself*.
**English drops it** where other languages keep it.

cards.title: Self-damage is the clearest case in English
cards.text: Every game distinguishes damage you take from an enemy and damage you did to yourself. So does the grammar.
points: **"He healed himself."** Target and caster are one.
**"He healed the team."** Different target.
**Same verb, different object.**
**The -self word is the target.**

cards.title: Good spot to pause
cards.text: Grammar done. Part 2 is the windmills — the most famous thing in the book. Your place is saved.

cards.title: The Adventure with the Windmills
cards.text: Thirty or forty windmills on a plain. This is the scene everybody knows even if they have never opened the book.

cards.title: Giants with enormous arms
cards.text: He tells Sancho that fortune is guiding them, and that he intends to fight and kill every one of them.
points: **Sancho says plainly: they are windmills.**
**Those are the sails**, not arms.
**Don Quixote rides at them anyway.**
**Sancho warns him again.** He does not stop.

cards.title: The sail lifts him and drops him
cards.text: The wind rises. A sail catches his lance, shatters it, and drags horse and rider across the field.
points: **The lance is destroyed.**
**Rocinante and Don Quixote both go down hard.**
**Sancho arrives and finds him unable to move.**
**It is a total, uncomplicated defeat.**

question.text: What does Don Quixote take the windmills to be?
question.explain: Giants with long arms. Sancho tells him they are windmills before he charges, and he charges anyway.

cards.title: He blames the enchanter Freston
cards.text: He says the wizard turned the giants into windmills at the last moment. It was done to rob him of the glory.
points: **Not "I was wrong."**
**"Somebody changed them to spite me."**
**This is the enchanter excuse from Week 5**, again.
**Nothing that happens can reach him.**

cards.title: This is why the phrase exists
cards.text: "Tilting at windmills" means attacking an imaginary enemy. One scene in one book, and four hundred years later it is a common phrase.
points: **A picture people remember** beats an argument.
**Sancho was right and it changed nothing.**
**Being told the truth** is not the same as accepting it.
**The scene works because we can see both versions.**

question.text: After being knocked down, Don Quixote admits the giants were windmills.
question.explain: False. He says an enchanter turned them into windmills to steal his glory.

terms.def: A -self word acting as the object, where the subject and object are the same.
The same word used only for emphasis. It can be removed.
Take the -self word out. If the sentence breaks, it was reflexive.
The person or thing the verb acts on.
Attacking an imaginary enemy. The phrase comes from this chapter.
The enchanter Don Quixote blames for turning the giants into windmills.

cards.title: The four that matter
points: **Reflexive: subject and object are the same person.**
**Delete it. If the sentence breaks, it was reflexive.**
**English drops it** where other languages keep it.
**Sancho was right, and it changed nothing.**

options: A -self word acting as the object, where subject and object are the same
A -self word used only for emphasis
A word that replaces a noun in any position
quiz.explain: Doer and receiver are the same person, and the -self word is doing real work as the object.

quiz.text: Which sentence uses a reflexive pronoun?
quiz.explain: Taught who? Himself is the object. In the other three the word can be removed.

quiz.text: How do you tell a reflexive pronoun from an intensive one?
options: Delete it. If the sentence breaks, it was reflexive
Check whether it is singular or plural
Look at where it appears in the sentence
See whether it ends in -self or -selves
quiz.explain: An intensive pronoun is removable. A reflexive one is the object, so removing it leaves a gap.
quiz.objective: Explain how a reflexive pronoun differs from an intensive one

quiz.text: Complete it: "The children helped ___ to more rice."
quiz.explain: Themselves. The children are both doing the helping and receiving it.
quiz.objective: Use reflexive pronouns correctly as objects

quiz.explain: I is the subject and the promise was made to the same person, so it is myself.
quiz.objective: Use reflexive pronouns correctly as objects

quiz.text: Which sentence is wrong in English?
quiz.explain: English does not use a reflexive with feel. Many other languages do, which is why this is a common error.
quiz.objective: Recognise verbs that do not take a reflexive pronoun in English

quiz.text: "He got himself up early" is standard English.
quiz.explain: False. "He got up early" is the natural form. English drops the reflexive with this verb.
quiz.objective: Recognise verbs that do not take a reflexive pronoun in English

quiz.text: What does Don Quixote believe the windmills are?
quiz.explain: Giants with long arms. The arms are the sails, as Sancho tells him before the charge.
quiz.objective: Retell the windmills episode and explain what Don Quixote concludes

options: A sail shatters his lance and drags him down
Sancho pulls him back in time
quiz.explain: The wind rises, the sail catches the lance, and both horse and rider are thrown across the field.
quiz.objective: Retell the windmills episode and explain what Don Quixote concludes

quiz.text: How does Don Quixote explain his defeat?
options: An enchanter turned the giants into windmills
He says the wind was unfair
quiz.explain: He names the enchanter Freston, who he says did it to rob him of the glory.
quiz.objective: Retell the windmills episode and explain what Don Quixote concludes

quiz.text: Sancho warns him that they are windmills before he charges.
quiz.explain: True, and more than once. Being told the truth is not the same as accepting it.
quiz.objective: Retell the windmills episode and explain what Don Quixote concludes

quiz.text: What does the phrase "tilting at windmills" mean?
quiz.explain: It comes straight from this chapter, and it has outlasted almost everything else in the book.
quiz.objective: Retell the windmills episode and explain what Don Quixote concludes

teacher.summary: Week 7 English covers reflexive pronouns alongside the windmills episode, matching the Term 1 weekly scope. It is deliberately the other half of Week 6: same eight words, different job, and the selfPronouns figure is reused so the contrast is made with the identical diagram rather than a new one. The deletion test is the whole method and is stated three times on purpose. The section on verbs that take no reflexive in English is included because it is where speakers of most other languages go wrong, and it is worth naming rather than leaving to instinct. NOTE ON THE TEXT: the school's edition is abridged and does not match Cervantes' chapter numbering, so this lesson follows the episode named in the title.
discussion: Ask him to run the deletion test on five sentences from anything he is reading. It takes two minutes and settles the topic.
Ask what changes between 'he trained' and 'he trained himself'. The reflexive makes it deliberate.
Ask why Sancho telling the truth made no difference. That question is most of what the book is about.
Ask him where he has heard 'tilting at windmills'. It is one of the few phrases from a novel that everyone uses.
teacher.extension: Have him write the windmill scene twice, once from Don Quixote's point of view and once from Sancho's, using reflexive pronouns in both. Two accounts of one event is the whole technique of the chapter.
misconceptions: 'Reflexive and intensive pronouns are different words.' They are the same eight words doing two different jobs.
'If it ends in -self it is reflexive.' Only if it is the object. Delete it and see whether the sentence survives.
'I feel myself tired is more emphatic.' It is not English. Feel takes no reflexive here.
'Don Quixote realises his mistake after the windmills.' He blames an enchanter. Nothing that happens reaches him.
